lead: Entropy is the property that turns the second law into arithmetic. The Carnot cycle shows that δQ<sub>rev</sub>/T sums to zero around any reversible loop, so that ratio depends only on the end states — it defines a state function S. Once you can compute ΔS, you can decide whether a process is possible, because the entropy of an isolated system never falls. Chemical engineers use this to test whether a proposed separation, heat-exchanger network or liquefaction train can work at all, and to measure how much work a real plant throws away.
prereq: You need: the Carnot cycle, the first law and the idea of a state function from the first-law chapters, and the ideal-gas relations from PVT behaviour and equations of state.

sections.h3: Entropy is a state function built from δQ<sub>rev</sub>/T

blocks.text: In the Carnot cycle (see Carnot cycle), heat QH enters at TH and QC leaves at TC. For a reversible cycle the efficiency is 1 − TC/TH, and the energy balance then gives QH/TH = QC/TC. Taking heat leaving as negative, the sum around the cycle is zero: Σ δQrev/T = 0.

Any reversible cycle can be sliced into thin Carnot strips, and each strip obeys the same result. So ∮δQ<sub>rev</sub>/T = 0 for every reversible cycle. A quantity whose cyclic integral is zero is a state function, the same test that makes internal energy a property. This one is called entropy, S.

blocks.where: dS is the change in entropy of the system (J/K); δQ<sub>rev</sub> is the small heat added along a reversible path (J); T is the absolute temperature of the system in kelvin at which that heat crosses.

blocks.text: For a finite change, ΔS = ∫₁² δQ<sub>rev</sub>/T, and the value depends only on states 1 and 2, never on the route. S is extensive, measured in J/K; per mole it is J/(mol·K), per kg J/(kg·K). Reversible heat divided by temperature is the whole definition — nothing about 'disorder' is needed at this level.

sections.h3: Calculating ΔS for the cases you meet

blocks.text: Because S is a state function, choose any convenient reversible path between the same two states. If the real path is irreversible, use a substitute path made of simple pieces.

blocks.where: C<sub>V</sub> is the molar heat capacity at constant volume, J/(mol·K); R = 8.314 J/(mol·K) is the gas constant; V₁ and V₂ are initial and final volumes; T is in kelvin.

C<sub>P</sub> is the molar heat capacity at constant pressure, J/(mol·K); P₁ and P₂ are initial and final pressures; T is in kelvin. The minus sign comes from the relation T dS = dH − V dP. For an ideal gas dH = C<sub>P</sub> dT, so dividing by T gives dS = C<sub>P</sub> dT/T − R dP/P; raising the pressure at constant T therefore lowers the entropy.

blocks.text: With constant heat capacity these integrate to ΔS = C<sub>V</sub> ln(T₂/T₁) + R ln(V₂/V₁) and ΔS = C<sub>P</sub> ln(T₂/T₁) − R ln(P₂/P₁). For an isothermal ideal-gas expansion the temperature terms vanish and only the volume or pressure term survives.

blocks.where: ΔH is the latent heat of the phase change in J/mol at temperature T in K (melting, boiling or sublimation). The sign of ΔH carries the sign of ΔS.
the second form holds for a solid or liquid heated with constant C<sub>P</sub> and no phase change; T₁ and T₂ are in kelvin.

items: Fix the end states and write down their T, P and V.
Break the path into constant-T, constant-P or constant-V pieces.
Apply the matching formula to each piece.
Add the pieces, keeping signs: melting is positive, condensation negative.

blocks.text: Real cycles are irreversible. Compare any such cycle with a reversible one working between the same two reservoirs at T<sub>H</sub> and T<sub>C</sub>. The real efficiency is lower, so Q<sub>C</sub>/Q<sub>H</sub> > T<sub>C</sub>/T<sub>H</sub>, and with rejected heat counted negative the cyclic integral drops below zero.

blocks.where: δQ is the heat crossing the system boundary (J); T is the absolute temperature of the reservoir or boundary where that heat crosses, in K; the integral runs over the whole cycle. Zero means a reversible cycle, negative means irreversible, positive is impossible.

blocks.text: This is the Clausius inequality. Some syllabi call it the mathematical statement of the second law, because it converts the words of second-law statements into a number you can evaluate for any proposed device.

blocks.where: the process form, for a change from state 1 to state 2; T is the temperature of the boundary where δQ crosses, in K. Equality holds only for a reversible path. When the boundary temperature is a constant T₀ this reduces to ΔS<sub>system</sub> ≥ Q/T₀.

blocks.text: Now apply it to a system plus its surroundings at T₀. The surroundings exchange heat reversibly, so their entropy change is −Q/T₀, and the inequality rearranges to ΔS<sub>system</sub> − Q/T₀ ≥ 0, that is, ΔS<sub>universe</sub> ≥ 0. For an isolated system, ΔS ≥ 0, with equality only when everything inside is reversible.

blocks.where: Sgen is the entropy generated by irreversibility, J/K; it is zero for a reversible process and positive for every real one. The work lost because of it is the theme of lost work and ideal work.

figure.caption: The two worked examples: 1 mol of ideal gas goes from 10 L to 20 L at 300 K, once along the reversible isotherm and once by free expansion. ΔS of the gas is 5.76 J/K both times because S is a state function; only the free expansion generates entropy.

examples.question: One mole of an ideal gas at 300 K expands reversibly and isothermally from 10 L to 20 L. Find the heat added, the entropy change of the gas, and the entropy change of the surroundings.
steps: Reversible isothermal expansion of an ideal gas: ΔU = 0, so Q<sub>rev</sub> = W = nRT ln(V₂/V₁).
ΔS<sub>gas</sub> = Q<sub>rev</sub>/T = 1728.8 J / 300 K = 5.76 J/K. Cross-check with R ln(V₂/V₁) = 8.314 × 0.6931 = 5.76 J/K.
The gas takes this heat from the reservoir, so ΔS<sub>sur</sub> = −1728.8/300 = −5.76 J/K, and ΔS<sub>universe</sub> = 0, as it must be for a reversible process.
examples.answer: Q<sub>rev</sub> = 1728.8 J, ΔS of the gas = 5.76 J/K, and ΔS of the surroundings = −5.76 J/K.
examples.check:
import math
R = 8.314
T = 300.0
n = 1.0
V1, V2 = 10.0, 20.0
Q = n * R * T * math.log(V2 / V1)
print(round(Q, 1))
print(round(Q / T, 2))
print(round(-Q / T, 2))

examples.question: The same 1 mol of ideal gas at 300 K now expands from 10 L to 20 L freely into an evacuated, insulated space (a free or Joule expansion). Find Q, W, ΔS of the gas, ΔS of the surroundings and S<sub>gen</sub>.
steps: Insulated, so Q = 0; expansion into vacuum, so W = 0; then ΔU = 0 and the ideal gas stays at 300 K.

The end states (300 K, 10 L) and (300 K, 20 L) are the same as in the first example. S is a state function, so use that reversible isothermal path as the substitute: ΔS<sub>gas</sub> = nR ln(V₂/V₁) = 8.314 × 0.6931 = 5.76 J/K.
The real path exchanges no heat, so ΔS<sub>sur</sub> = 0.
S<sub>gen</sub> = ΔS<sub>gas</sub> + ΔS<sub>sur</sub> = 5.76 J/K > 0: the free expansion is irreversible. Note that the real ∫δQ/T = 0 is less than ΔS = 5.76 J/K, as the Clausius inequality demands.
examples.answer: Q = W = 0, ΔS<sub>gas</sub> = 5.76 J/K, ΔS<sub>sur</sub> = 0 and S<sub>gen</sub> = 5.76 J/K.

traps: Using the real irreversible heat in dS = δQ/T. The actual Q/T is not the entropy change; compute ΔS along a reversible substitute between the same end states.
Putting the system temperature instead of the boundary temperature in ∮δQ/T. For an irreversible process the T belongs to the reservoir where the heat crosses.
Swapping the signs of the two ideal-gas forms: the volume term is +R ln(V₂/V₁), the pressure term is −R ln(P₂/P₁). Using plus with pressure gives the wrong sign in compression.
Forgetting that freezing and condensation have negative ΔS, because their ΔH is negative and ΔS = ΔH/T keeps that sign.
Unit slip: R = 8.314 J/(mol·K) gives ΔS in J/K. With R = 0.08314 L·bar/(mol·K) the answer would be in L·bar/K, which is not an entropy unit you can add to J/K.

quiz.q: Define the entropy change for a reversible path.
quiz.a: dS = δQ<sub>rev</sub>/T, so ΔS = ∫₁² δQ<sub>rev</sub>/T along any reversible path between the states. Unit: J/K.

quiz.q: Why does ∮δQ<sub>rev</sub>/T = 0 prove that entropy is a state function?
quiz.a: A quantity whose integral around every closed path is zero depends only on the end states. That is the definition of a state function, so S can be tabulated like U and H.

quiz.q: Two moles of an ideal gas are heated at constant volume from 300 K to 600 K. Find ΔS. C<sub>V</sub> = 12.5 J/(mol·K).
One mole of saturated water vapour condenses at 373 K and 1 atm. ΔH<sub>vap</sub> = 40.66 kJ/mol. Find ΔS.
quiz.a: Condensation releases heat, so ΔH = −40 660 J/mol. ΔS = ΔH/T = −40 660/373 = −109 J/(mol·K).

quiz.q: A cycle takes 100 kJ from a 500 K reservoir, delivers 30 kJ of work and rejects 70 kJ to a 300 K reservoir. Evaluate ∮δQ/T and comment.
quiz.a: ∮δQ/T = 100/500 − 70/300 = 0.200 − 0.2333 = −0.0333 kJ/K. Negative, so the cycle is irreversible but possible; a positive value would make it impossible.

quiz.q: What does the Clausius inequality say for an isolated system?
quiz.a: Use the process form ΔS<sub>system</sub> ≥ ∫δQ/T. An isolated system exchanges no heat, so the right side is zero and ΔS<sub>isolated</sub> ≥ 0, with equality only when every change inside is reversible. The cyclic form ∮δQ/T ≤ 0 is about a complete cycle; it is not the same object as ΔS.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry ΔS comes from steam tables and equation-of-state software, not hand integrals. Entropy generation is the working currency of exergy audits of plants. Search for "exergy analysis" and "Gouy–Stodola theorem".
